subject: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values

messages.author: 6a15c5567bc065f7
messages.subject: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values
parts:
Hi All,

First of all, I tried to follow the SEMNET link provided here often (http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html) for general SEM questions, but it didn't lead anywhere... So I appreciate if you can help me despit the non-rogram specicific question.

QUESTION1:
In my model I get good CFI, RMSEA and SRMR values, despite P-value of Chi-square (Test Statistic) is non-significant. Same for the RMSEA P-value.
How am I to interpret the results. From here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/lavaan/p-value/lavaan/QBgAHrBo_08/nxbdIBY6DAAJ) I get a hint that I can rely on CFI, RMSEA and SRMR despite the P-values, but I am hesitant.

QUESTION2:
I also get an error message (see in the results: covariance matrix of latent variables
                is not positive definite), and I am not sure if I should worry about it give the acceptable fit indices.

See my code and results below and thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values
parts:
A non-significant p-value indicates good fit. So, if the other fit indices do as well this is consistent.

However, I do wonder about sensibility of estimating 37 parameters when n = 51 and that may be responsible for your error. I find it alarming to fit a model with so many parameters when your sample size is so small.

messages.subject: Re: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values
parts: If you are fitting a regular CFA model I believe your code should be:

HS.model <- ' 
F1 =~ H2 + H3 + H5 + H6 + H9 + H12

F2 =~ H16 + H15 + H19 + H17 + H21 + H26
        '
It doesn't like you need a mean structure either. Try changing these and see if you still get a warning.

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values
parts:
Following Christopher

  1. Ideally you have closer to 5 or more people for every variable, so your model is too complex for so few people. See Costello, A. B., & Osborne, J. W. (2005). Best practices in exploratory factor analysis: Four recommendations for getting the most from your analysis. Practical Assessment Research & Evaluation, 10(7), https://scholarworks.umass.edu/pare/vol10/iss11/17.

  2. The warning message means no matter how well your model fits, it’s wrong. The covariance matrix is not positive definite. That usually means you have estimated too many factors for so few people. Usually you would need 12 items per factor to get a solution with only 50 people. See

Marsh, H. W., & Hau, K. T. (1999). Confirmatory factor analysis: Strategies for small sample sizes. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Statistical strategies for small sample research (pp. 251-284). London: SAGE Publications.

Marsh, H. W., Hau, K.-T., Balla, J. R., & Grayson, D. (1998). Is more ever too much? The number of indicators per factor in confirmatory factor analysis. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 33(2), 181-220. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr3302_1

2020. február 19., szerda 1:31:26 UTC+1 időpontban Gavin T. L. Brown a következőt írta:

Following Christopher

  1. Ideally you have closer to 5 or more people for every variable, so your model is too complex for so few people. See Costello, A. B., & Osborne, J. W. (2005). Best practices in exploratory factor analysis: Four recommendations for getting the most from your analysis. Practical Assessment Research & Evaluation, 10(7), https://scholarworks.umass.edu/pare/vol10/iss11/17.

  2. The warning message means no matter how well your model fits, it’s wrong. The covariance matrix is not positive definite. That usually means you have estimated too many factors for so few people. Usually you would need 12 items per factor to get a solution with only 50 people. See

Marsh, H. W., & Hau, K. T. (1999). Confirmatory factor analysis: Strategies for small sample sizes. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Statistical strategies for small sample research (pp. 251-284). London: SAGE Publications.

Marsh, H. W., Hau, K.-T., Balla, J. R., & Grayson, D. (1998). Is more ever too much? The number of indicators per factor in confirmatory factor analysis. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 33(2), 181-220. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr3302_1
